items.title: Germany wants to manufacture American PAC-3 interceptors to help meet global demand
items.author: Sebastian Sprenger
items.summary: German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has lobbied U.S. defense leaders to allow the production of PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles in Germany.
items.body:
COLOGNE, Germany — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has lobbied U.S. defense leaders to allow the production of PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles in Germany, arguing an additional production site would help alleviate a glaring shortfall in the global supply chain for the vital air-defense weapons.

Pistorius’ comments in Berlin on Wednesday offer more details about an agreement struck with his U.S. counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon last week.

The German defense minister said the spirit of that accord reflects Berlin’s willingness to manufacture all elements of the Patriot value chain — PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors, launchers and all — in Germany, plus whatever other American weaponry is in short supply among allies.

Germany’s MBDA already makes PAC-2 interceptors, a Raytheon product. The more advanced, and more expensive, PAC-3 MSE interceptors, on the other hand, are made by Lockheed Martin, which has a longstanding cooperation agreement in Germany with Rheinmetall, including in the missile sector.

Whether PAC-3 production in Germany or elsewhere in Europe will come to pass is largely a matter of the U.S. government and Lockheed Martin playing along. Details would likely also depend on the scope of work happening abroad.

The performance characteristics of Patriot interceptors are a closely guarded secret, as that information could allow adversaries to build countermeasures into their attack missiles. There is also a business decision wrapped up in the export of Patriot production, as the equipment has been a decades-old cash cow for the manufacturers and the U.S. government alike.

Ukrainian leaders said in July they were promised by U.S. President Donald Trump that they would be able to make Patriot interceptors under license in Ukraine, though the details of that arrangement remain unclear.

Patriot interceptors are a key defense against Russian missiles that have been battering Ukrainian cities.

Sebastian Sprenger is associate editor for Europe at Defense News, reporting on the state of the defense market in the region, and on U.S.-Europe cooperation and multi-national investments in defense and global security. Previously he served as managing editor for Defense News. He is based in Cologne, Germany.

items.title: Fast-paced funding for force-protection innovation
items.summary: UKDI seeks counter-Uncrewed Aerial System capabilities for development to deployment
items.body:
UKDI has launched a new Themed Competition called Project PANOPTES which seeks an integrated, Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System ( C-UAS ) force-protection capability

Open to UK based innovators

This Themed Competition is run on behalf of the Ministry of Defence ( MOD )

A share of £5 million is available immediately

The Competition deadline has been extended to midday 30 September 2026 ( BST ) due to an update to the Competition Key Requirements table.

Applicants are advised to review the revised Competition Key Requirements table again before submitting.

The competition team will contact anyone who has already submitted a proposal, or who has a proposal in draft, to advise on next steps.

UK Defence Innovation ( UKDI ) is pleased to launch a new Themed Competition called Project PANOPTES . Run on behalf of the Ministry of Defence ( MOD ) this Themed Competition seeks an integrated, Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System ( C-UAS ) force-protection capability.

This competition will use a 2-stage submission process with the aim to ease the burden on both applicants and assessors. Stage 1 provides an initial innovation screening process where applicants outline their idea. Stage 2 then requests detailed proposals on successful ideas by invite.

Learn more about the 2-stage process in the Competition Document.

Defence is seeking innovations to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly relevant for deployed land forces but is also applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure.

Existing approaches are constrained by current capability, high costs, limited manoeuvrability and the pace of evolving UAS. To ensure the UK maintains a battle-winning edge, UKDI is seeking ideas that can solve these problem areas.

What we are seeking

Your solution should protect deployed troops against complex attacks designed to overwhelm existing infrastructure and munition stocks. It should deliver a more affordable response to emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and be capable of autonomous operation. The MOD is interested in a range of innovative and credible solutions including, but not limited to, Laser Directed Energy Weapons (LDEWs) effectors.

The solution should also consider:

integration with a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV)

integration with a future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capability

possible export opportunities

Learn about the full requirements in the Competition Document.

A launch webinar will take place on 9 September 2026 to provide further detail on the operational context of the problem space and a chance for attendees to ask questions in an open forum. If you would like to participate, please register on the Eventbrite page .

Please ensure you have read the Competition Document fully before attending.

Submit a proposal

If you have a capability that could protect deployed troops and our munition stocks head to the Competition Document to submit your idea.

items.title: Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth's speech at the UK Space Power Conference
items.summary: Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth delivered the opening keynote of the UK Space Power Conference, setting out how the UK will defend its interests in space.
items.body:
Well, good morning, everyone. I think I am in control of the PowerPoint. There we go. The Minister has just said to me it’s boiling up there so I’m glad I wore my woollen Spitfire suit.

It’s really good to see so many distinguished guests, colleagues, allies and friends here and welcome to the UK Space Power Conference here in what is a relatively unexpected sunny London, which is great. It’s so good to see lots of familiar faces in the audience – I’m slightly worried that there’s a sea of light blue at the back there to hold me to account on what I’m about to say.

But I’m particularly glad to see so many new faces and to meet so many new characters from across the space enterprise, scientists, academics, industry experts. We’ve got some leaders in finance and of course, there is a good group here from across government. So thank you all for supporting the conference. I really do from a personal perspective, I appreciate that.

I stood here just a few months ago alongside many of my fellow international air and space chiefs at what was the Global Air and Space Chiefs Conference. And then I outlined how the RAF is now formally on a journey to becoming Europe’s first sixth generation air force with the Global Combat Air Programme and now our new Collaborative Combat Air programme, the Storm Fighter, operating alongside F-35, Typhoons and a range of many other autonomous systems. But these capabilities will never fulfil their potential without space. And that’s why these conferences and this discussion over the next two days are so very important.

From my perspective, I don’t think I can get to a sixth-generation air force if I still have a fourth-generation space force. And that is a topic that I’m hoping we can cover over discussions in the coming two days. Space is obviously a prerequisite for modern air power. Every element of a sixth-generation air force depends intimately on space, the networks, the targeting, the navigation, the command and control.

Space is no longer just simply supporting air power from the sidelines. It is completely embedded within it. It is essential. It’s actually part of the DNA and you don’t have to scratch too far to see that. And space is no less relevant to the other domains. The effective use of space is critical to the ability of our new integrated force to understand, to communicate, to move and to fight. And as we learn critical lessons from ongoing conflicts in places like Ukraine and the Middle East, it is clear that a pivot to uncrewed systems is required at pace.

And of course, if we’re going to do this, an uncrewed force is broadly a space-dependent force, once again reinforcing the importance of this vital domain to defence. We often refer to space as the ultimate high ground, through which the integrated force gains a decisive operational edge, enabling it to act with greater speed, better precision, and overall better effectiveness. It is an advantage we must maintain, and if possible, deny to our adversaries.

Space services are not just the invisible thread between our ships at sea, our soldiers on the land and our aircraft in the skies. They now completely underpin our whole approach to strategic deterrence, command and control, and decision advantage. And more broadly, across the fabric of our society, space underpins our modern way of life.

Just coming here, being linked to space told me, if I don’t hurry up, I’m going to be late. And the Air and Space Commander was panicking, thinking he was going to have to do this keynote. It’s been six years since I was appointed as the first director of space for the MOD, as Anu mentioned. Space was an important topic then, but I would argue now it is a critical matter which must be better understood and better championed across the whole of government, specifically if we are serious about our approach to modern deterrence. It is our responsibility to make sure that everyone in defence knows that the integrated force will not succeed without space. Space must become embedded in how defence generates and operates force.

To reflect this, the Royal Air Force’s headquarters at RAF High Wycombe transitioned to become Air and Space Command just a few weeks ago. I’m sure some of you saw that announcement. This is more than just a simple name change. We are demonstrating that space is no longer just a supporting function. Space is now seen as a warfighting domain in its own right and with equal importance to the other domains.

It is a contested, congested and competitive environment where our operational edge and strategic advantage can be won but can also be very quickly and easily lost. Space can no longer be delayed, no longer deferred, or delegated. It must now be delivered and that has been my big message into our own department on this topic.

But importantly it cannot be delivered via national means only and we know in UK we cannot do this alone and I’m delighted that we are joined today by so many international colleagues from around the globe. Our greatest strength is our coalition of space partners spanning the world, an alliance that is envied and feared in equal measure by our potential adversaries, with all members bringing different capabilities from unique geography to unique on-orbit assets, making our collective security greater than the sum of the space parts.

In the UK, NATO is of course our most critical alliance. And whilst we are building sovereign space capabilities, these will always be part of a NATO force, always part of our strategic deterrence approach. NATO led the way by recognising space as a domain in 2019. And two years later, NATO expanded the scope of our collective defence policy, making it clear that attacks to, from, or within space present a clear threat to the alliance and could possibly trigger an Article 5. This was a major statement of intent. In short, an attack on one of us in space is an attack on all of us, just as it is in the other, more traditional domains.

And whilst UK strategy is NATO first, we are not only NATO. Earlier this April, I went to Colorado to meet with my counterparts from 10 other nations, from the USA in the West to New Zealand in the East for the Principals Board of the Combined Space Operations Initiative, or CSpO. There we agreed to redouble our efforts to deliver capabilities in support of combined space operations, creating a web of global space power, generating and delivering mutually supportive capabilities that no adversary can match. Again, a fundamental approach to our collective deterrence posture.

And central to this is Multinational Force Operation Olympic Defender. This is now our primary international operational framework within which we deliver responsible, combined space operations, and these are happening on a very routine basis at this very moment.

Last September, we delivered the first ever UK-US space operation under the banner of OOD. We completed a Rendezvous Proximity Operation in geostationary orbit, moving one of our SKYNET satellites close to a satellite operated by US Space Command. 35,776 kilometres from Earth’s surface, to be precise. These satellites were traveling at 11,000 kilometres per hour. That’s 3 kilometres per second. So, a collision would most definitely be catastrophic, creating substantial, long-standing debris in an orbit that is congested, full of critical assets.

That is why operations like this must only ever be delivered with the utmost of care, with the utmost of precision, communication, expertise and most importantly, collaboration and agreement. When another nation manoeuvres their satellite close to ours without collaboration, that is unacceptable. It is dangerous and it is unprofessional. It is no different than flying an aircraft to within 50 feet of my aircraft without coordination.

Unfortunately, we are now seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries in flagrant disregard of the norms for responsible behaviour by space-faring nations. In May of this year, we tracked a series of unusual and significant manoeuvres by 5 Russian military satellites, moving to within rapid reach of two finished commercial satellites. These manoeuvres were uncommon and dangerous, raising serious questions about Russia’s intent in space. And the next month, in June, it was confirmed that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across the breadth of Europe, Greenland and Canada over at least 75 days since 2019.

We all know and we all rely on GPS. It’s an excellent system operated by our colleagues in the US Space Force. It is used by billions of people and industries around the world and of course it’s used by many global military forces. Major disruption to GPS would cost the UK economy to the tune of £1.4 billion of impact every day. Sat-Nav systems would fail, congestion on the roads would create havoc. Our emergency services would take much, much longer to reach those in need.

So make no mistake, the satellite services you may have taken for granted now face unprecedented threats. And losing these services, be it the Sat-Nav that keeps ups moving, the timing signals for financial transactions, the Earth observation that allows us to monitor the weather or the effects of climate change. All of this would make every sector sitting in this room less efficient, less prosperous and less secure.

Our adversaries know this. They are developing sophisticated space systems and they have both the capability and the intent to use them. Last year, and most of you will know this handsome chap, last year, the commander of UK Space Command, Tedders (ret. Major General Paul Tedman) here today. He’s not. He knew I was putting this picture up. So our previous commander of UK Space Command denied that Russia is attempting to jam UK military satellites with ground-based systems every week. At the same time, Germany’s defence minister said that Russia had been shadowing their military satellites. Alongside grey zone activity across all domains, space is a region of growing strategic competition. Space has become a warfighting domain, whether we like that or not. And the UK, as well as its partners and allies, must be prepared for this.

Fortunately, this is now recognised across government here in the UK. And in June of last year, we had the Strategic Defence Review, it outlined that space remains a critical national infrastructure sector. Space underpins 20% of the UK’s GDP. In real money, that’s almost £500 billion. But it is also a site of growing competition. The SDR set out the MOD’s requirement to invest in space control decision advantage, reconnaissance, navigation, and timing signals. And if the SDR set out what we in defence would call the ends, this year’s defence investment plan set out our means.

And I just heard the Minister for Space talk about the DIP. £9 billion of new space capability already earmarked for 2030 to 2035. And from this year to 2030, £2.3 billion for satellite communications, £880 million for space-based ISR and space control, and a further £440 million for novel space technology. And now we have a new UK Space Strategy issued just this month. A strategy that outlines how the UK government will act as one regards space, making our nation a competitive space power, assertive in protecting our interests and driving our own economic growth. To protect the nation and also to help it prosper is MOD’s aim.

Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives. And our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them. We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace. At the heart of the UK space arsenal and a major offer to our global alliance is Skynet and many of you in this room will know of our Skynet programme and the capability that offers. It’s the backbone of UK’s sovereign global comms capability and provides command and control for our entire integrated force.

And I’m grateful that the Defence Investment Plan allocated an additional £50 million to extend the life of our in-service SKYNET 5 satellites. And these will be joined next year with the launch of our new SKYNET 6 series, SKYNET 6A. While our demand for SATCOM only increases, and as threats in space grow more serious, SKYNET will be supplemented with allied and commercial SATCOM services. These will provide additional capacity, coverage, and resilience, with resilience being the keyword. Using both SKYNET and commercial SATCOM, UK armed forces will be able to make and communicate decisions quickly around the world. And this is an incredibly important keystone of our quest for decision superiority in today’s modern warfare.

And the decision-making of our integrated force will be further improved by space-based intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. Through our ISTARI programme, we’re delivering a constellation of satellites to provide a multi-sensor, multi-spectral capability to observe activity on the Earth, day or night, heat wave or snowstorm. One of these satellites, the Tyche, is now in space. Over the next two years, three more will be launched: Titania with in-space missions, Juno with SSTL, and Oberon with Airbus Defence Space.

ISTARI will feed our nascent digital targeting web, which in itself has been allocated £1.8 billion under the DIP, an initiative which will truly make our armed forces a single integrated force, connecting sensors, deciders, and effectors driving speed and how we decide to degrade or destroy an identified target in any domain underpinned by world leading AI and software. Our integrated force also relies on these services, so we must monitor them.

We deliver this through world leading sensors, both military and commercial, on the ground and in space. and many of you will recognise these pictures, including RAF Fylingdales, the UK’s primary military space sensor, and the only three-faced and foreign-operated radar in the US space surveillance network. Alongside Fylingdales, we will have our new deep space advanced radar capability, the DARC, a trilateral programme with sites in Australia, the UK, and the USA, enabling us to detect, identify, and trap objects in the deepest of orbits.

But Fylingdales and DARC aren’t simply radars. They too are part of the integrated battle management architecture, forming part of defence’s pervasive multi-domain sensor network. NOCTIS 2, the first sovereign UK sensor for our National Space Ops Centre, or the NSPOC, declared fully operational capability this year. This high-precision optical sensor system, developed in partnership with Spaceflux, is now observing the vital satellites we rely on for military ops around the world. NOCTIS 1 will be soon followed by NOCTIS 2, another advanced sensor which will achieve even higher rates of precision and fidelity.

And we are building the infrastructure for these sensors to be modular, changeable and transportable. So we can swap out and move them as strategic demand evolves. This way, our space domain awareness capabilities would be agile, integrated and ready to support the integrated force anywhere in the world. And unsurprisingly, we will establish more advanced sensors to enhance our SDA using cutting edge technology.

This includes neuromorphic sensors which will help search for unexpected activity around our own satellites. Neuromorphic technology will allow us to monitor large volumes of space with drastically reduced power consumption, latency and data bandwidth, allowing us to detect events in orbit whilst increasing both our global sensor footprint and our observation capability.

However, it isn’t all about the sovereign sensors and what we’re building within the military. Commercial data procured from our industry partners will always be part of the hybrid, flexible and resilient SDA effort. This year, many of us will have avidly and I’m sure excitedly kept on top of the groundbreaking Artemis II mission. The first crewed Artemis flight and the first lunar flyby since 1972. Our team in the NSPOC using data from Spaceflux tracked this historic mission, demonstrating easily just how we can monitor significant events in orbit using the sensors and the data from our space industry partners.

The value of commercial data for our space domain awareness is shown day in and day out by the Joint Commercial Ops Initiative, the JCO. The JCO programme now encompasses over 20 nations with the JCO UK team and UK Space Command leading the Meridian region between the Americas to our west and the Pacific to our east. JCO teams worldwide are providing unclassified information on activity in orbit, strengthening integration with the commercial sector and integrating public information into military operations. But this SDA will be of limited value unless we can convert it into effective decision making. And so this year, our BOREALIS command, control and data processing system developed by CJI as part of a five-year, £65 million contract reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule. I don’t often get to say that.

This system used by No.1 Space Ops Squadron in the NSPOC is providing timely, quality information to government and military commanders, allowing us to make effective decisions and provide operational understanding of the space domain to the whole of the integrated force. Through all of these capabilities, space is now the connective tissue of that integrated force and we must protect these vital capabilities from the threats we see growing every day. This month’s new UK Space Strategy outlined the UK’s Control of Space requirement.

Through a whole of government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests, we will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.

But we are not doing this for its own sake. We’re doing this to enable our own freedom of action and for that of NATO and for our overall security. We’re protecting the command and control of our integrated force by defending global strategic communications and the systems that generate our decision advantage and combat edge. To help our nation fulfill the control of space requirement, UK defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.

This can be described as actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives, electronic warfare and capabilities to counter anti-satellite weapons. Alongside other supporting operations, these capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.

To deliver these capabilities, I am incredibly proud today to announce that we are forming No. 3 Space Effects Squadron, UK defence’s first dedicated squadron to deliver operations in support of the UK’s Control of Space mission. No. 3 SES will disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.

The squadron will be staffed by specialist personnel from across defence and will support offensive and defensive space operations, safeguarding the critical space services which are so incredibly precious to us.

But with all of this said, let’s be very clear, and this is particularly important for this audience. No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.

Alongside our colleagues across government, we aim to promote norms, rules and responsible behaviours in space so that space is preserved as a safe, secure and sustainable domain for prosperity, research and exploration. Our approach to control of space will always be transparent and rooted in international collaboration and norms.

We will never escalate military activity in space, but we must respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment in which threats to our critical space systems are growing every single day.

UK Space Command and its associated Space Squadrons operating under the newly established HQ Air and Space Command will deliver space power to protect this nation. We already have No. 1 Space Ops Squadron working as part of the NSPOC and No. 2 Space Warning Squadron delivering the operational activity that we all know so well from our RAF Fylingdales. Our new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will deliver precise, integrated effects to safeguard our national interests in space. And we are planning more. Numbers 4, 5 and 6 Squadrons, including a Space Tactics and Training Squadron, and squadrons which will deliver the deep space advanced radar capability. And a Space Defence function working as part of the newly established Integrated Air, Space and Missile Defence Operations Centre.

The Strategic Defence Review gave us the ends. We’ve discussed that here. The Defence Investment Plan gave us the means, and I’ve talked to some of those numbers. Together though, I think we are all the ways.

And it is time for us to harness our resources. It is time to get moving. It’s time to act. and it’s time to deliver more meaningfully with our space capabilities.

To work with all of you to turn our approved budget lines into real, tangible capability so that we can monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.

Thank you very much indeed and thanks again for supporting us.

items.title: RAF launches first ever space squadron dedicated to defending Britain's satellites
items.summary: The RAF has launched No. III Space Effects Squadron, its first dedicated unit to counter hostile threats to UK satellites.
items.body:
New No. III Space Effects Squadron will be the UK’s first unit dedicated to disrupting, degrade, and deny hostile threats in space.

The squadron will protect the critical satellites that guide British ships, connect mobile phones and warn of missile attacks.

Forms a key part of the UK’s ability to gain and maintain freedom to operate in space, as set out in the government’s Space Strategy published this month.

Satellites vital to everyday life in the UK are set to be protected from hostile threats, as the RAF launches the UK’s first ever dedicated space squadron focused on disrupting, degrading, and denying enemy activity targeting British interests in space.

Announced today by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smith at the first-ever UK Space Power Conference, No. III Space Effects Squadron will bring together specialist personnel from across the Armed Forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the nation depends on every day.

While sister units No. I Space Operations Squadron and No. II Space Warning Squadron give the RAF the ability to watch and warn of threats in space, the new No. III Squadron will act against those threats, using advanced technology, including Electronic Warfare, to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions. The squadron will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service.

It comes as the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will give a keynote address at the Space Conference.

He is expected to say:

Britain has to keep pace in the new space race. Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th century deterrence. That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space. Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth. My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.

In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.

Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth.

My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.

Satellites are a core part of national security and support daily life across the UK. They are critical to intelligence gathering and missile warning, but also power mobile phone data, weather forecasts and online ordering. Ambulances, firefighters and the police rely on satellite navigation systems for emergency responses, and energy networks use the same systems to organise power grids.

As space becomes more crowded and more dangerous – with hostile states developing capabilities to jam, disrupt or disable space assets – the government is taking action to defend UK interests in space, while maintaining an operational advantage for our armed forces.

The Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said:

Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.

Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost.

No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.

The formation of No. III Space Effects Squadron contributes to the UK’s developing capabilities for space warfare, including Electronic Warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons.

The work delivers on the UK’s Control of Space Requirement - the need to maintain freedom to operate in space, and deny adversaries the same freedom. The Requirement was set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month, and builds on the Strategic Defence Review, which made clear that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins the UK’s security, prosperity and daily way of life.

While taking action to protect critical space infrastructure, the government remains committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space.

The UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and continues to work through the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours.

That commitment underpins the UK’s continuous work with allies and partners to strengthen collective defence in space, including an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance and space control activities.

items.title: Okinawa chiefs don covers, receive anchors
items.author: PO2 Zachary Guth
items.summary: Okinawa welcomed its newest members to the rank of chief petty officer at Keystone Theater on Kadena Air Base on Sept. 16, 2026. Nineteen Sailors were pinned to chief petty officer alongside five U.S. Marines and one U.S. Air Force Airman as honorary chief petty officers.
items.body:
KADENA AIR BASE, Japan – Okinawa welcomed its newest members to the rank of chief petty officer at Keystone Theater on Kadena Air Base on Sept. 16, 2026. Nineteen Sailors were pinned to chief petty officer alongside five U.S. Marines and one U.S. Air Force Airman as honorary chief petty officers.

The chief pinning ceremony represents the culminations of six weeks of physical, mental and emotional training. Families and mentors were welcomed on stage to pin the fouled anchor onto the new chiefs and don them with the chief petty officer cover. For the first time in their career, they bear the uniform of a chief petty officer.

“Six weeks did not magically turn you into a chief. A chief is built, with time, with mistakes, long nights, hard lessons, difficult conversations, and repeated reminders that the job is bigger than your ego,” said Command Master Chief Frank Queenlacombe, Naval Mobile Construction Battalion 5 senior enlisted leader, during his remarks. “Today is not the finish line. It is your second beginning, your second birthday.”

Two of the 19 Sailors selected for promotion to chief petty officer on Okinawa belong to Commander, Fleet Activities Okinawa’s security department.

“I am incredibly grateful to reach this milestone at CFAO, surrounded by fellow chiefs and officers who have made a lasting impact on my career and the Sailor I have become,” said Chief Master-at-Arms Brandon Hodges. “I wouldn’t be here without the people who have believed in me, pushed me to grow and supported me throughout this journey. Their guidance and support have meant more to me than I can put into words.”

In total the chief pinning ceremony brought together six naval commands across the island of Okinawa, along with the five Marine commands and one Air Force command. Together, they forged their leadership, their ideals, communicated with their mentorship and laid the groundwork for a new chapter in their lives.

“You don’t change who you are because you become a chief, it only enhances you,” said newly pinned Chief Sonar Technician (Submarines) Tony Holman, assigned to Navy Data Center Detachment Okinawa. “You go from being a leader by yourself, to understanding that you can’t do it alone. That you’re not a chief to just your Sailors but to everybody.”

The Navy rank of chief petty officer holds special regard amongst the U.S Armed Forces, a tradition going back 133 years, with those selected moving into roles of great responsibility and leadership. With the striking of two bells and the whistle of the boatswain’s pipe, the chiefs carry the weight of the anchor as they salute the side boys for the first time.

“The chief petty officer pinning is a public display of an outward, visible dedication—an acceptance of the responsibility to provide servant leadership to the sons and daughters whom we are entrusted to lead into harm’s way every day,’ said Command Master Chief Aaron Belcher, Commander, Fleet Activities Okinawa senior enlisted leader, after the pinning ceremony. “We achieved this through the support of everyone along our journey and the relentless hard work of our Sailors.”

He concluded, “Ultimately, the pinning ceremony provides total transparency into the expectations of a chief, serving as a public dedication to being present, meaningful leaders on the deck plates."

items.title: MAG-24 Marines train with Army, Air Force to rapidly repair damaged airfields
items.author: Sgt Anabelle Reedobrien
items.summary: MARINE CORPS TRAINING AREA BELLOWS, Hawaii — Sept. 14-17, 2026, service members from Marine Wing Support Squadron 174, Marine Aircraft Group 24 trained with the Army’s 130th Engineer Brigade and the Air Force’s 647th Civil Engineer Squadron to sharpen the joint force's ability to rapidly repair damaged airfields. This joint training strengthened interoperability and readiness, enhancing the U.S. military's ability to operate in austere environments.
items.body:
MARINE CORPS TRAINING AREA BELLOWS, Hawaii — Sept. 14-17, 2026, service members from Marine Wing Support Squadron 174, Marine Aircraft Group 24 trained with the Army’s 130th Engineer Brigade and the Air Force’s 647th Civil Engineer Squadron to sharpen the joint force's ability to rapidly repair damaged airfields. This joint training strengthened interoperability and readiness, enhancing the U.S. military's ability to operate in austere environments.

Runways are critical to aviation operations in any environment. During a crisis, the speed that repair crews respond can determine how quickly flight operations resume. This joint airfield damage repair (JADR) exercise involved a realistic scenario with service members assessing and repairing large craters simulating the kind of damage that may be encountered in contested environments. After assessing and clearing out the damaged areas, service members used a special form of rapid-setting cement to repair the simulated craters.

“This training impacts the Marine Corps in a lot of ways,” said 2nd Lt. Zachary Kolb, JADR officer in charge, with MWSS-174. “Working with partnered forces prepares us for future operations while giving the Marines a realistic exercise that covers all aspects of airfield damage repair.”

While technical proficiency was a key focus, the broader value was in standardizing the process across military branches and preparing participants for future operations. Participating units coordinated their efforts through a shared command post, emphasizing teamwork alongside technical proficiency. The joint structure enabled the services to align planning, streamline communications and synchronize their distinct technical procedures.

“It’s always a great experience working with different branches,” said Lance Cpl. Mark Rummel, a combat engineer, with MWSS-174. “It's eye-opening to learn how they operate and their unique strategy for getting the mission done.”

As the dust settled over Marine Corps Training Area Bellows, Marines, soldiers and Airmen packed their gear with a clearer understanding of how their specialized capabilities support the joint force. By working together to solve complex logistical challenges, they refined a standardized approach to repairing damaged airfields giving commanders more reliable options to rapidly restore flight operations and project airpower from remote locations in contested environments.

items.title: Ritsumeikan University students have lunch with CLR 37 Commanding Officer
items.author: Cpl Anakin Smith
items.summary: U.S. Marine Corps Col. Robert Gerbracht, commanding officer of Combat Logistics Regiment 37, 3rd Marine Logistics Group, hosted approximately 20 students from Ritsumeikan University in Kyoto, Japan, for lunch at the Mess Hall on Camp Kinser, Okinawa, Japan, Sept. 15, 2026.
items.body:
CAMP KINSER, Okinawa, Japan — U.S. Marine Corps Col. Robert Gerbracht, commanding officer of Combat Logistics Regiment 37, 3rd Marine Logistics Group, hosted approximately 20 students from Ritsumeikan University in Kyoto, Japan, for lunch at the Mess Hall on Camp Kinser, Okinawa, Japan, Sept. 15, 2026.

The visit allowed students to experience life aboard a military installation, have a better understanding of the purpose and mission of the U.S. military in Japan, and be able to interact with Marines. The visit was personally significant to Gerbracht, who attended Ritsumeikan University from 2009 to 2011.

“It was great to see them, not only as student from the same university but as people”, said Gerbracht. “We’re able to interact with a whole new generation of students that are there and get to share an experience with them.”

Gerbracht and his wife were both selected for the Olmstead Scholar Program, a military education program that awards scholarships to highly qualified, active-duty junior officers in the United States military in order to pursue language studies and overseas graduate-level education. The scholar program provides one year of foreign language training followed by two years of study at a foreign graduate school.

“My wife and I both applied in 2008”, said Gerbracht. “We actually ended up being the first married couple to be selected for the Olmsted program.”

Students with Ritsumeikan University traveled from mainland Japan to Okinawa as part of a university culture trip to the island, and it is frequent that this trip includes a visit to Camp Kinser. The students got to sit down with Marines while aboard the base, allowing them to learn more about each other's ways of life.

“I spoke with some of the students about the differences between Japanese culture and American culture.” said Gerbracht. “But there's also a lot of similarities between what we value as Marines and what a lot of Japanese people value.”

During his time at Ritsumeikan University Gerbracht earned his master's degree in international relations. Learning the language and experiencing the culture has helped Gerbracht in his current position as commanding officer a forward-deployed logistics regiment as well as base commander of the Urasoe-based Camp Kinser, in addition to paying dividends at his other duty stations as well.

“The way you lead better is by having a broad base of knowledge.” said Gerbracht, “It’s like having 1,000 keys to locks you haven’t seen yet.”

items.title: The KC-130J: Past, present and the future fight
items.author: CPT Rebekah Harasick
items.summary: Operation Slingshot demonstrated the KC-130J's current ability to enable critical power projection for the Marine Corps, using its heavy payload capacity to leapfrog ahead of F-35B fighter jets. The KC-130J lands at remote, undeveloped airfields to establish Aviation-Delivered Ground Refueling and re-arming points. During this self-supported movement, the KC-130J traversed a route from Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal, Australia, through Cairns, Pohnpei, the Kwajalein Atoll, and Wake Islan
items.body:
In the vast, unpredictable Indo-Pacific, islands dot the expanse of the sea for miles. Close enough to be a positive, yet far enough apart and sparsely populated to qualify as austere. This part of the world doesn't provide an answer to accessibility, and that question gets even foggier when you employ strategy and tactics.

But 3d Marine Aircraft Wing (MAW) has an answer: the KC-130J, an aviation platform built for this exact venture. Operation Slingshot is a proof-of-concept strategy hailing from historic times when the Corps used island-hopping to win wars, and although aviation platforms are sleeker and more technologically advanced today, the need for Marines across the globe has not changed. The KC-130J's ability to extend reach gives pilots the ability to strike fast and move faster as they conduct "the slingshot." In this part of the world, it is not just an advantage; it is a necessity.

For the 3d MAW KC-130J, demonstrating expeditionary capabilities across thousands of miles of ocean requires more than the fighter jets you see in Top Gun. It requires a lifeline.

During Operation Slingshot, the KC-130J successfully projected 3d MAW, along with F-35B Lightning II fighters, across 4,000 nautical miles of the Indo-Pacific, into locations secured by Marines using MV-22B Ospreys and other components of the wing.

Drawing on a legacy established during the siege of Khe Sanh and Operation Desert Storm, the KC-130J operated as a self-contained logistical node, establishing forward refueling points without reliance on external strategic tankers.

Since its introduction, the C-130 platform has served the United States military and the Marine Corps as the logistical backbone of aviation. Originally birthed out of necessity during the Korean War, its inception after the maiden flight in Marietta, out of the Lockheed-Georgia Company facility in 1955, marked the start of a new era. During the 1968 siege of Khe Sanh in Vietnam, C-130s lived up to their designed intent, delivering over 12,000 tons of supplies via paradrops, austere landings and keeping the surrounded 26th Marines supplied when overland routes were severed. Decades later, during Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Marine KC-130s continued to demonstrate that same prowess with extended capabilities, providing the critical aerial refueling necessary to increase the range of strike packages deep into the northern Persian Gulf. The KC-130J solidified its position in aviation through enhanced multi-mission functionality, all while retaining the transport versatility of its roots.

Today, the Indo-Pacific theater demands the same endurance and adaptability, updated for the modern battlefield. Operation Slingshot demonstrated the KC-130J's current ability to enable critical power for the Marine Corps, using its heavy payload capacity to leapfrog ahead of F-35B fighter jets. The KC-130J lands at remote, undeveloped airfields to establish Aviation-Delivered Ground Refueling and re-arming points.

During this self-supported movement, the KC-130J traversed a route from Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal, Australia, through Cairns, Pohnpei, the Kwajalein Atoll, and Wake Island, terminating in Hawaii. By ferrying the necessary Marines, gear, and fuel, the KC-130J allowed the F-35Bs to slingshot deeper into the theater.

"While the jets are focused on the tactical fight, the KC-130J is the workhorse in the background, carrying the maintainers, the maintenance equipment, and the fuel required to dramatically extend the range and lethality of those jets," said 1st Lt. Christian Schwien, a KC-130J co-pilot.

Transforming the KC-130J into a moving, forward logistics hub requires precise integration across the crew. Pilots execute long-range over-water navigation and land the 135,000-pound aircraft on austere strips. In the cargo hold, loadmasters manage weight, balance, and high-stress air-delivered ground refueling operations.

The KC-130J remains positioned to support the missions of tomorrow whether they be winking amidst a sea of blue to the east in the Indo-Pacific or concentrated down under from Australia. In an era where near-peer dynamics and global geopolitics continue to evolve, 3d MAW’s need endures for a versatile platform, one capable of unlocking future operational possibilities while honoring the legacy of aviation feats that define its historic past.

items.title: Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation. The post Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, though other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.

The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.

The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.

“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.

To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:

- Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores

- Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.

- Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.

- Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.

- Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering

- Routine updates and briefings to Congress on these issues

The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.

In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.

The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.

The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.

Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.

“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.

The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.

Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.

“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”

A Numbers Game

The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.

But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.

“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”

Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.

“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.

And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”

“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”

Breaking a Stalemate

The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm, now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.

“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”

Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.

What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.

This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.

“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”

“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.

That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.

“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.

Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.

“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”

While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.

“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.

For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.

“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”

items.title: US Navy destroyers tested in Middle East as demands mount
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: The concentration of Navy destroyers in the Middle East raises questions about meeting sustained operational demand.
items.body:
Navy destroyers are concentrated in the Middle East as U.S. forces conduct operations against Iran, according to U.S. Central Command — a move that puts renewed operational demands on a fleet that has experienced prolonged maintenance periods.

As of Sept. 14, two Navy guided-missile destroyers were operating in the Red Sea and another 13 were in the Arabian Sea, according to the U.S. Naval Institute’s fleet tracker, which uses both Navy and public data.

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Stout also departed Naval Station Norfolk on Monday to begin deployment operations after months of training, maintenance and certification events, according to Naval Surface Force Atlantic.

The demand facing the class has been significant, even before the start of the Iran war.

The USS Carney spent 235 days deployed from September 2023 to May 2024 and conducted 51 engagements against Houthi-launched weapons, according to the Navy. The campaign demonstrated what operations around one of those chokepoints can demand from destroyers.

When USS Carney returned in May 2024, then-Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Lisa Franchetti told the crew that the last time the Navy had directly engaged an enemy to that degree was during World War II.

The renewed demand for destroyers in the Middle East comes as the Navy’s maintenance system has struggled to keep the fleet on schedule.

U.S. Fleet Forces Command declined to discuss its current destroyer readiness posture, current operations or potential effects on future deployment schedules, citing operational-security and classification guidelines. The command also declined to provide historical aggregate data on destroyer operational tempo.

According to a December 2025 Congressional Budget Office analysis of Navy maintenance data, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer overhauls that began between 2011 and 2024 took an average of 26% longer than the Navy’s final schedules estimated.

The 225 DDG-51 overhauls CBO analyzed also required 8% more labor than scheduled.

CBO projected that DDG-51 destroyers will spend an average of more than nine years, or about 27% of their planned service lives, in maintenance. That is more than twice the roughly four years envisioned in the Navy’s 2012 class maintenance plans.

The federal budget agency identified several factors contributing to longer maintenance periods, including the aging fleet, postponed maintenance, late inspections and contract awards, unexpected additional work, delays in parts and materials and modernization work.

The average age of the DDG-51 fleet rose from 10 years in 2011 to 20 years in 2024.

The Government Accountability Office has found broader problems across the Navy’s conventional surface fleet.

In a January 2025 review, GAO found that the Navy requested nearly $24.9 billion for combat-surface-ship maintenance from fiscal 2020 through 2023 and reported that nearly $25.9 billion was appropriated. The Navy reported obligating 99.7% of that funding by the end of fiscal 2023. Yet, GAO found that the service continued to face shortages of spare parts, insufficient qualified maintenance personnel and a continuing need to defer maintenance.

CBO’s analysis covers maintenance events beginning in 2011 and points to longstanding factors, including the age of the destroyer fleet and postponed work.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

items.title: Investigators Blame F-16 Thunderbird Crash on Turned Fan Blade Deep in Engine
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: A misaligned vane in an F-16 engine that field-level maintainers cannot see to inspect caused one of the U.S. Air Force's Thunderbird jets to crash last December, a new report concludes. The same problem led another F-16 to crash 20 months earlier. The post Investigators Blame F-16 Thunderbird Crash on Turned Fan Blade Deep in Engine appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
A misaligned vane in an F-16 engine that field-level maintainers cannot see to inspect caused one of the U.S. Air Force’s Thunderbird jets to crash last December, a new report concludes. The same problem led another F-16 to crash 20 months earlier.

The pilots ejected in both cases, escaping with minor injuries, while both jets were total losses. Separate Air Force Accident Investigation Boards came to similar conclusions.

The report on the Dec. 3, 2025, Thunderbird crash in the California desert was released Sept. 21. The report on the prior crash, on April 30, 2024, near Holloman Air Force Base, N.M., was released months before the Thunderbird crash, in February 2025.

The latest investigation report valued the loss of the Thunderbird F-16 at $33.5 million.

Both accidents were blamed on turned variable vanes deep in the Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-220 engine’s high-pressure compressor. Investigators determined that one or more vanes were turned and misaligned, creating “abnormal aerodynamic forces” and “irregular wake patterns” as air flowed through the engines. The resulting stress on compressor blades caused vanes to break or crack, casuing the engines to “catastrophically” fail.

The Thunderbird investigation report cited three known instances where compressor blades fractured due to turned vanes, but it did not specify a third instance. Besides the Holloman crash in 2024 and the Thunderbird crash in 2025, no publicly released Accident Investigation Board reports from the last decade mention fractured compressor blades in the F100-PW-220.

In both the Holloman and Thunderbird cases, field maintainers failed to catch the misaligned vanes. While some stages can be inspected with a borescope, the fifth stage of the engine core cannot be seen in the F100-PW-220 without completely disassembling the engine core.

Notably, both F-16 engines in question had experienced foreign object debris, or FOD, events in the years prior to the crashes. The Thunderbird jet engine’s FOD event occurred in October 2021, and the Holloman F-16’s FOD event happened in August 2022. In both cases, maintainers noted damage to early stages of the inlet fan but found no issues with the fourth, seventh, or eighth stages, which they could inspect using a borescope.

The Air Force’s technical orders for the F-16 do not require maintainers to remove and disassemble the engine core to inspect those stages after a FOD event if no damage is found in the surrounding stages. It’s unclear if the FOD events caused the vanes to turn, however, so cannot be clearly blamed for triggering the events.

The accident investigation board for the Holloman F-16 crash noted that Pratt & Whitney’s analysis determined the FOD event was the probable cause of the vane turning, but expert opinions varied when asked if it was possible for damage to occur to a later stage if no damage was observed in the ones before it. That left the cause inconclusive.

Similarly, the board for the Thunderbird crash noted that it was “impossible to conclusively determine” what caused the turned vanes. It did, however, note that the lack of inspection for the fifth and sixth stages after a FOD event “substantially contributed to the mishap.”

“The post-FOD event guidance contains an inherent inability to inspect these specific sections of the engine core. Additionally, the core of the engine is only inspected during scheduled maintenance when a core component reaches its overhaul threshold, leaving time for potential damage to progress undetected,” the report states.

A spokesperson for the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately comment on whether the technical guidance might be changed to require complete inspections following a FOD event or to trigger other steps to prevent similar mishaps. In February 2025, after the report for the Holloman crash was released, the spokesperson said the center’s F-16 program office “is looking at this issue and is working closely with the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Propulsion Directorate, the engineering authority for the engine, to correct any deficiencies.”

‘Ejecting Was Ultimately the Only Option’

In addition to detailing the engine issues, the Thunderbird report detailed how the pilot did everything possible to save the jet.

An experienced instructor pilot with nearly 1,400 flight hours, the pilot was on a routine training flight working on loops and rolls and flying from the Thunderbirds’ famed “delta formation.” The mishap pilot had planned to peel off from the formation during the loops to avoid exacerbating a stiff neck, then rejoin the formation for the rolls. But as the pilot waited to rejoin, the engine stalled. It felt “like the jet just … stopped midair,” the pilot told investigators.

Seeking to recover, the pilot sacrificed speed to gain altitude, then tried a secondary engine control. When that didn’t work, the pilot attempted an engine restart. “It sounded like things were grinding,” the pilot reported later. Finally, more than four minutes after the engine stalled, the pilot chose to eject.

The Accident Investigation Board concluded that “ejecting was ultimately the only option which provided a favorable outcome.”

Yet the ejection wasn’t flawless—the F-16’s ACES II ejection seat has two hoses that transfer hot gas from the ejection initiators to the sequence valves, and they’re supposed to disconnect automatically during an ejection. One of the hoses in the Thunderbird F-16 didn’t disconnect properly but ripped from the violence of the ejection.

The plane went down near Trone, Calif., a small desert community near Death Valley. Upon impact, debris scattered up to 750 feet away. A local civilian who saw the crash got to the pilot first, and Navy search and rescue responded within minutes to transport for medical care. The pilot was discharged the same day.

items.title: Space Force Seeks Maneuverable Spacecraft for On-Demand Launch
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force may invest in a maneuverable space vehicle that can be available for an on-demand launch in response to “emerging threats,” according to a new industry notice. The post Space Force Seeks Maneuverable Spacecraft for On-Demand Launch appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Space Force may invest in a maneuverable space vehicle that can be available for an on-demand launch in response to “emerging threats,” according to a new industry notice.

In a Sept. 18 request for information, Space Systems Command’s Space Safari program office—which leads the service’s Tactically Responsive Space program—said they’re interested in buying a commercial spacecraft that can perform what are known as rendezvous proximity operations and dock to other satellites. The notice specifies a potential need for the capability as soon as fiscal 2029.

“[The] Space Safari program rapidly acquires, integrates, and deployed space systems to address urgent combatant commander needs and emerging threats outside traditional programs of record,” the notice states. “To achieve this, the office seeks innovative, cost-efficient solutions for unpredictable mission requirements.”

The notice doesn’t spell out how many of these vehicles the Space Force might buy but identifies a target “tasking-to-launch” timeline of 14 days. It also stresses the need for modular systems that can integrate a variety of payloads should the service need to swap a system at the last minute.

The Space Force defines Tactically Responsive Space, or TacRS, as the ability to quickly respond to on-orbit threats in any number of ways—from launching a rocket on demand to maneuvering an at-the-ready satellite to replace or augment another to buying commercial space capabilities during a conflict.

Space Safari has been demonstrating and progressing new TacRS capabilities over the last few years. In 2023, Firefly’s Alpha rocket launched a Millennium Space Systems payload just 27 hours after receiving launch orders as part of the service’s Victus Nox mission. Then in late 2025 and early 2026, it conducted a tabletop effort and field exercise called Victus Diem aimed at refining its processes for repeatable rapid launch.

In June, the service launched Victus Haze, which focused on validating multiple TacRS concepts, including dynamic space operations between two satellites. In this case, a Rocket Lab satellite launched on demand and a True Anomaly spacecraft prepositioned on orbit took turns playing the role of adversary and conducting “dynamic engagements” including pursuits between the two satellites.

Those demonstrations have put the service on a path toward operationalizing TacRS concepts. The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget request, which includes $86 million for TacRS demonstrations, says Space Safari plans to use funding to support “operational missions requiring both rapid launch and maneuverable, prepositioned capabilities.”

The documents also note that the Space Force plans to establish a “rapid reaction force structure” that would involve having satellites in production and on hand, ready for rapid launch as needed. The Sept. 18 notice appears to be an early step in that direction.

In a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power Col. Bryon McClain told reporters the service is in the process of transitioning TacRS into an “operational system.” He noted that while the Space Force has additional missions planned, it would likely be saying “less and less” about them.

“You’re probably going to hear a lot less about that overall because we see this as an important warfighting capability, and the last thing you want to do is make that too public,” he said Sept. 16.

For now, the five known TacRS missions expected to launch in the next few years are:

- Victus Surgo, a mission cosponsored by the Defense Innovation Unit that will feature a SpaceX Falcon 9 launching a highly maneuverable spacecraft built by Impulse Space

- Victus Salo 1, set to launch in 2027 on a Falcon 9 rocket that will carry a payload built by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

- Victus Salo 2 and 3, which don’t yet have a public timeline but will involve Impulse Space’s pre-positioned Mira orbital maneuver vehicle

- Victus Sol, launched by Firefly’s Alpha, which will carry an operational payload

items.title: 8,000 Airmen and Guardians Still Have Medical Shaving Waivers After Policy Changes
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Around 8,000 Airmen and Guardians currently have medical waivers exempting them from shaving—thousands less than just a few years ago but still about half of all the waivers across the U.S. military. The revelation comes shortly after the Department of the Air Force started directing commanders to consider separating those who have had medical shaving profiles for too long. The post 8,000 Airmen and Guardians Still Have Medical Shaving Waivers After Policy Changes appeared first on <a hre
items.body:
Around 8,000 Airmen and Guardians currently have medical waivers exempting them from shaving—thousands less than just a few years ago but still about half of all the waivers across the U.S. military. The revelation comes shortly after the Department of the Air Force started directing commanders to consider separating those who have had medical shaving profiles for too long.

All of the services are currently refining their policies to align with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 2025 mandate that medical shaving waivers be limited to 12 months and those with permanent conditions be evaluated for separation.

Details on the number of waivers have been scarce to this point. But this week, Task & Purpose reported that “as many as 16,300” service members have these waivers. That includes 4,760 Sailors, 3,400 Soldiers, and 144 Marines.

The other 8,000 are Airmen and Guardians, a Department of the Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine. These individuals have “an active temporary medical shaving waiver,” the spokesperson said. They did not immediately provide a breakdown of the waivers between the Air Force and Space Force.

The Air Force currently has about 495,300 Airmen, and the Space Force has roughly 10,400 uniformed Guardians—meaning about 1.6 percent of service members in the department have a waiver.

That’s down significantly from “historical averages” of 18,000 to 20,000 Airmen and 300 Guardians, the department spokesperson said. Military.com has previously reported that the number of medical shaving waivers in the Air Force went from 13,131 to 23,068 between 2021 and 2023.

The department spokesperson noted that the recent drop in waivers was due to “recent policy updates and clinical reevaluations.”

Still, the total number of shaving wavers in the Air Force and Space Force is disproportionally larger than the other services, a reality that could create manning challenges if a large number of those waiver holders wind up being involuntary separated in the future.

The medical shaving waiver total does not include Sikhs, Muslims, and other religious groups who have been permitted to wear beards and other facial hair in uniform under religious accommodations. Hegseth has directed that service members who wear beards under religious accommodations be reevaluated under the pre-2010 appearance standards that generally do not authorize facial hair waivers.

In early August, the DAF directed commanders to begin to consider separating Airmen and Guardians who have held shaving profiles for more than 12 of the past 24 months and who remain unable to conform to grooming standards.

Commanders must either initiate involuntary separation or submit a retention recommendation to their chain of command. Airmen and Guardians separated “solely on the basis of the condition” and not for deliberate disregard of the policy will receive an honorable discharge, the guidance states. Commanders should not use the new policy to separate members who otherwise would be separated for unsatisfactory performance or misconduct, according to the guidance.

In some cases, Airmen and Guardians with medical waivers unable to meet the new facial hair standards could be eligible for retention. Commanders have the option to submit retention recommendations to their chain of command, according to the guidance, which adds that approval could be granted on a “case-by-case” basis if there is a “compelling government interest” for retention, such as:

- Low manning and retention rates in the Airman or Guardian’s career specialty

- The Airman or Guardian has special experience or specialized training

- The cost and time required to replace the individual is extensive

- The Airmen or Guardian is close to retirement

Gas Mask Seal Test

In late August, the DAF also released instructions that gives all Airmen and Guardians until Dec. 31 to verify they can achieve a proper protective mask seal, a new requirement Hegseth announced last year as part his crackdown on service members with beards, goatees, and other facial hair.

All Airmen and Guardians must complete a CBRN Defense Foundations Course, an annual web-based course taken through DAF e-Learning. Then they have to achieve a proper protective mask seal by the year-end deadline. The test must be witnessed by a “mask fit validation monitor,” which will be appointed at the Air Force and Space Force squadron level.

Hegseth’s Sept. 30 memo states that “noncompliant personnel—due to refusal, exemption denial, or failed tests—will be flagged as nondeployable in the appropriate Military Service personnel system. Repeated noncompliance may result in administrative separation.”

The CBRN training and mask-seal validation are slated to become annual requirements for Airmen and Guardians.
